source.title: Towards Benchmarking Privacy Vulnerabilities in Selective Forgetting with Large Language Models
source.authors: Wei Qian; Chen-Xu Zhao; Yangyi Li; Mengdi Huai

record.file_problem: The text presents the paper through its references and is not visibly cut off or garbled.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates knowledge leakage after unlearning with different attacks and measures, including fine-tuning, quantization and prompt/data perturbations, rather than reproducing a single original unlearning experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper reports knowledge-leakage results for unlearned LLMs that bear on recovery by fine-tuning, quantization and prompting/data perturbation. It does not test activation-direction ablation or show that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge. It does not establish a near-chance threshold for unlearned knowledge or measure general ability in these attack experiments. Membership-inference and data-reconstruction results, and cited findings, are outside the claim versions. Figure-only values are retained as figure only rather than assigned to individual bars.
record.test_reason: A benchmark that reruns published recovery attacks on GA/NPO/RMU-unlearned LLMs. Fig. 5 uses Zephyr-7B-beta on WMDP-Bio and WMDP-Cyber, with fine-tuning on three data sources and quantization. Fig. 7a uses Llama-3-8B on RWKU with five-shot, translation, prefix and adversarial-suffix prompts. Figs. 6c, 6d and 9 test robust-unlearning defenses (NPO+SAM, TAR, AdvNPO, AdvRMU) against these attacks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that unlearned models leak knowledge under fine-tuning (more than quantization) and under prompt perturbations, and that combining attacks increases leakage. Existing defenses generally lack robustness and are sensitive to attack sample count; data-perturbation attacks are easier to defend than model-perturbation attacks.
record.recipe_differences: The paper benchmarks multiple unlearning methods (GA, NPO and RMU) and applies existing leakage attacks; it is not a reproduction of a single original method or recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery differs by attack and data perturbation: fine-tuning generally outperforms quantization, partial unlearning data typically outperforms external or retain data, optimization-based data perturbations tend to outperform static methods, and SAM weakens as attack sample count increases.
record.problems: Claim-related plotted values are not numerically available in the provided text; the text gives qualitative conclusions instead. It does not establish the near-chance criterion or report a general-ability check for these recovery experiments. Individual attack and defense values in several figures cannot be assigned from the flattened figure text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports knowledge-leakage results for combined perturbing-unlearned-data and partial-data fine-tuning attacks in Fig. 3, and image perturbations on CIFAR-10 in Fig. 7b. These were omitted because figure-specific values and condition assignments are not recoverable from the provided flattened figure text. Membership-inference and data-reconstruction results were left out because they do not measure the recovery behaviors named in the versions.

untested.parts: General (retained) ability is not reported for the unlearned models.
Relearning-set sizes for the Fig. 5 attacks are not stated, so 'small' cannot be checked.
Entire version: no activation-direction ablation and no access-blocking vs deletion analysis.
Quantization bit width is not stated.
Jailbreaks in the usual sense and in-context provision of the forgotten information are not tested.
Robust methods other than NPO+SAM, TAR, AdvNPO and AdvRMU are not tested.

missing.what: Printed no-attack baselines: WMDP accuracy 0.240/0.260/0.289 (Bio) and 0.284/0.246/0.245 (Cyber); RWKU ROUGE 0.317/0.337/0.324. Needed to show a near-chance start.

record.verdict_notes: The reader claimed near-chance was not established, but Fig. 5 prints no-attack accuracies of 0.24-0.29 (chance 0.25). Translation is an other-language attack, so E covers it. Attacked values are figure-only; the states rest on the authors' prose. I dropped the reader's B limits_scope label: the text says all three fine-tuning sources recover, so a ranking among them does not qualify B. Fig. 3 (combined attacks) and Fig. 7b (CIFAR-10) are declared in rows_left_out. None of the original sources is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports recovery attacks but does not establish that targeted-knowledge accuracy was near chance before attack, or evaluate retained general ability.
It tests fine-tuning with external Openwebtext, retain data and partial unlearning data, but does not report a small relearning-set size in the presented text.
No activation-direction ablation, internal activation edit, or analysis establishing access-blocking rather than deletion.
The paper tests model quantization but the presented text does not state the quantization bit width.

It tests five-shot prompting, translation, static prefix injection and dynamic adversarial suffix optimization as data perturbations; it does not test jailbreaks, other-language prompting as a separately described attack, or in-context information beyond the named methods.
The paper evaluates defenses against specified attacks, but does not establish robustness against every attack in the claim or across all unlearning settings.
